# Superscripts and subscripts


<!-- WARNING: THIS FILE WAS AUTOGENERATED! DO NOT EDIT! -->

A superscript, such as `²`, is a mark written straight after a token
that applies an operation to it. A numeric subscript, such as `₁`,
selects positions from an array or axes for a function. Both bind more
tightly than any function. `v₁²` is the square of item 1 of `v`:

``` bpl
v←10 20 30
v₁²
```

    400

[Typing glyphs](glyphs.qmd#typing-glyphs) gives their keys. For bare
inverse `⁻`, type Alt-6, `-`, then Space. Alt-6 then `-1` gives `⁻¹`, a
negative power on numbers or a negative Rank on functions.

## Superscripts

### On an array

On an array, a superscript digit is a power:

``` bpl
x←3
≥x²
```

    10

A power of `¯1`, written `⁻¹`, is the reciprocal:

``` bpl
2⁻¹
```

    0.5

`ᵀ` swaps rows and columns:

``` bpl
m←[1 2
   3 4]
mᵀ
```

    1 3
    2 4

In `2 3²`, the superscript touches only the `3`:

``` bpl
2 3²
```

    2 9

In `[2 3]²`, it touches the whole list:

``` bpl
[2 3]²
```

    4 9

After a space, a superscript applies to the whole run on its left:

``` bpl
2 3 ²
```

    4 9

The run can be any expression, such as `≥x`:

``` bpl
≥x ²
```

    16

A strand of names is several runs, one for each name:

``` bpl
y←5
x y ²
```

    3 25

A spaced superscript also needs a space after it:

``` bpl
2 3 ² + 1
```

    5 10

### On a function

On a function, numeric superscripts specify [cell
ranks](glyphs/jot-diaeresis.qmd): `f¹` is `f⍤1`, `f⁰ ¹` is `f⍤[0 1]`,
and `f⁰ ¹ ²` is `f⍤[0 1 2]`. Adjacent digits form one rank (`f¹²` means
rank 12); spaces separate ranks. A negative rank counts back from the
argument’s rank, so `f⁻¹` works on cells with one fewer axis than the
argument. Unlike `⍤`, the short form needs no separator before a numeric
argument: `-⁰5`.

Here `+/¹` sums each row of `m`, `+⁰ ¹` adds one left scalar to each
right row, and `⌽⁻¹` reverses each row:

``` bpl
+/¹m
10 20+⁰ ¹m
⌽⁻¹m
```

    3 7

    11 12
    23 24

    2 1
    4 3

Bare `f⁻` is the inverse of `f`, the same as `f⍣¯1`. The minus has no
superscript digit immediately after it: `f⁻¹` is rank ¯1, while `f⁻ ¹`
applies the inverse at rank 1. Use `f⍣2` to repeat a function twice, not
`f²` (rank 2).

`f⁻ Y` gives the `X` for which `f X` is `Y`. Inverses follow BQN’s
[specification of inferred
properties](https://mlochbaum.github.io/BQN/spec/inferred.html). The
inverse of the exponential `*` is the natural logarithm:

``` bpl
*⁻1
```

    0

Monadic Encode, `⊤`, gives a number’s binary digits. Its inverse reads
the digits back into a number:

``` bpl
⊤⁻1 0 1
```

    5

In a dyadic call, `X f⁻ Y` is the `Z` for which `X f Z` is `Y`. The
inverses of `2×` and `2*` are division by 2 and the base-2 logarithm:

``` bpl
2×⁻10
2*⁻8
```

    5

    3

Inverting [Replicate](glyphs/hash.qmd#expand) puts fill where the mask
has zeros:

``` bpl
1 0 1#⁻10 20
```

    10 0 20

A superscript applies to the whole function on its left, as a monadic
operator does. `+\⁻` turns running sums back into the numbers they came
from:

``` bpl
+\⁻1 3 6
```

    1 2 3

The same goes for a derived function such as `-¨`:

``` bpl
-¨⁻1 2 3
```

    ¯1 ¯2 ¯3

A bound function such as `2↣×` inverts as a whole too:

``` bpl
2↣×⁻10
```

    5

Numeric superscripts just after a number remain powers: `+↢3⁻¹` adds a
third. Bare `+↢3⁻` would instead try to invert the number `3`, a
`DOMAIN` error. To invert a function that ends in a number, put the
function in parentheses:

``` bpl
(+↢3)⁻ 10
```

    7

A space before the superscript applies it to the whole preceding run, so
the parentheses can be left out:

``` bpl
+↢3 ⁻ 10
```

    7

With the axis operator, the inverse can also go before `⍠`. `#⁻⍠¯1` is
the same function as `(#⍠¯1)⁻`.

Inverses follow the rules of Power. They pass through bound arguments,
Each, Rank and the other compositions that Power lists. `f⁻←g`
[attaches](assignment.ipynb#inverses-and-derivatives) an inverse to any
function that a name holds.

[`ᵇ`, Bitwise](glyphs/superscript-b.qmd), is a monadic operator that
applies a Boolean function to integer bits. For example, `6∧ᵇ3` is `2ₓ`.

### A function as a scalar

`fᵘ` is a scalar holding the function `f`, as
[`⊂`](glyphs/left-shoe.qmd) encloses a subject. `⊂` can’t enclose a
function, because written next to one it forms a train. Like any scalar,
`+ᵘ` has an empty shape:

``` bpl
ρ+ᵘ
```

    ⍬ₓ

Its depth counts the one layer around the function:

``` bpl
≡+ᵘ
```

    1ₓ

### Errors

- `DOMAIN`: a function with no known inverse, `ᵀ` on a function, or `ᵘ`
  on an array
- `SYNTAX`: a superscript after a space that doesn’t stand alone, as in
  `2 3 ²+1`

## Subscripts

On an array, a subscript selects a major cell. `v₁` is `1⌷v`:

``` bpl
v₁
```

    20

A negative subscript counts from the end:

``` bpl
v₋₁
```

    30

A single subscript selects a matrix row. Numeric subscripts separated by
spaces form one coordinate: `m₁ ₀` is `m.[1 0]`. Touching digits form
one position: `v₁₂` selects position 12. Parentheses keep sequential
selections separate: `(a₁)₂` selects item 2 of item 1:

``` bpl
m₁
m₁ ₀
```

    3 4

    3

After a dotted path, a subscript selects from the whole path:

``` bpl
T←["a":[10 20]]
T.a₁
```

    20

With a space before it, a subscript selects from the whole run on its
left:

``` bpl
2 3 ₁
```

    3

As with a superscript, the run can be any expression:

``` bpl
≥v ₁
```

    21

If the first subscript is separated from its item, keep a space after
the coordinate too.

A subscripted item can be an assignment target:

``` bpl
v₁←5
v
```

    10 5 30

Modified assignment works too:

``` bpl
v₁+←1
v
```

    10 6 30

Use numeric subscripts for literal positions along successive axes. Use
[Index](glyphs/squad.qmd), `⌷`, or [bracket indexing](indexing.ipynb)
for computed positions, vectors of positions, keys or whole axes.

After a function, numeric subscripts choose axes, as
[Axis](glyphs/quad-colon.qmd) does. `+/₀` is `+/⍠0`, and `+/₀ ₁` is
`+/⍠[0 1]`:

``` bpl
+/₀m
+/₀ ₁m
```

    4 6

    10

In `f⁝x₁`, the subscript indexes `x` before the call. `(f⁝x)₁` indexes
the call’s result. An array of functions is still an array: `fs₁`
selects its item 1.

The subscript letters `ₓ`, `ⱼ`, `ₑ` and `ᵣ` are parts of numbers, as in
`3ₓ` and `1ᵣ3`. [Numbers](numbers.qmd) covers them. Between two items,
`ⱼ`, `ₑ` and `ᵣ` form one [number](numbers.qmd#writing-numbers): `xⱼy`
is `x+y×0ⱼ1`, and `xᵣy` constructs a rational from integer components. A
trailing `ᵣ` converts to the unbounded integer/rational domain: `3ᵣ`
means `3ᵣ1`, and a whole result stays in that domain. `÷ᵣ` selects
rational division before computing. Ordinary integer `÷` floors; `÷ₐ`
selects float division. After a name, or any item but a number or a list
of literals, `ₓ` floors to machine integers. `xₓ` is `⌊ₓx`:

``` bpl
x←3.7 ¯2.5
xₓ
```

    [3 ¯3]ₓ

After a function, `ₓ` floors its results to ordinary integers under
either `kinds` setting. [Numbers](numbers.qmd#static-kinds) gives the
static conversion rules.

`⌊ₓ`, `⌈ₓ` and dyadic `÷ₓ`, which floors the exact quotient as Python’s
`//` does and gives an ordinary integer, as `¯32768ₓ₂÷ₓ¯1ₓ₂` gives
`32768ₓ`, each compute their integers in one pass:

``` bpl
7 ¯7 7.5÷ₓ2
```

    [3 ¯4 3]ₓ

The sized integer markers `ₓ₁`, `ₓ₂`, `ₓ₄` and `ₓ₈` give fixed integers
occupying 1, 2, 4 or 8 bytes. The full digit run after `ₓ` is the width:
`ₓ₁₆` is invalid. Parenthesize a conversion before indexing, as in
`(vₓ₁)₂`. [Fixed-width integers](numbers.qmd#fixed-width-integers) gives
the conversion and promotion rules.

After a function, a sized marker converts the function’s results:

``` bpl
√ₓ₁ 17
```

    4ₓ₁

A float width’s marker, `ₕ`, `ₛ` or `ₚ`, works the same way. After a
function it makes the function’s results floats of that width, and after
an array it converts the array, as [`•float`](system/float.qmd) does:

``` bpl
-ₛ 3
xₛ
```

    ¯3ₛ

    [3.7 ¯2.5]ₛ

`ₐ` (approximate) converts to real floats. After an array, a complex
number gives its real part at its parts’ width, an exact number or a
Boolean gives a float of the default width, and a float keeps its width:

``` bpl
(3j4)ₐ
1r3ₐ
```

    3

    0.3333333333

After a pervasive function other than `√`, `⊛`, `*`, `○` and `○⁻`, which
keep their own real-part rule, `ₐ` converts the arguments to real floats
before the call, taking a complex argument’s real part, at the width
that their float promotion gives, never a width chosen from values:
`!ₐ25ₓ` computes in floats rather than in overflowing integers. After a
function that isn’t pervasive, such as `≢`, `ₐ` converts the results.
`÷ₐ` selects float division before computing, rather than converting a
floored integer quotient. Outside the real domain a result is the real
part of the principal value. `√ₐ¯4` is 0, the real part of `0j2`.
`¯8*ₐ÷3` is 1, the real part of the principal root 1+i√3. `√ₐ`, `⊛ₐ` and
`*ₐ` each run as one kernel. Under [`∂`](glyphs/partial.qmd), their
slopes are the real part’s. [Numbers](numbers.qmd#approximate) gives the
rules:

``` bpl
√ₐ¯4 9
¯8*ₐ÷3
```

    0 3

    1

### Errors

- `SYNTAX`: a subscript after a space that doesn’t stand alone, as in
  `2 3 ₁+1`, or that is an assignment target, as in `v ₁←5`
- `SYNTAX`: `₋` with no digit after it
- `SYNTAX`: `ⱼ` or `ₑ` beside a function or a space, as in `f←- ◇ fⱼ1`
- `LENGTH`: the item is a unit, which has no axis to select from
- `DOMAIN`: `ₓ` on a complex number

## Differences from APL

BPL also accepts Dyalog’s `x*2`, `f⍣2` and `f⍣¯1`. BQN writes the
inverse as `𝔽⁼`. Neither language has subscripts.
